explanations.explanation: That's what he finds, friend. The Teacher, son of David and king in Jerusalem (Ecclesiastes 1:1), writes that “in the place of judgment there is wickedness, and in the place of righteousness there is wickedness.” These are the two spots where you'd go looking for fairness. I'd be shaking my head too.

I get the hope, friend. You'd expect fairness in those two spots. But the Teacher, son of David and king in Jerusalem (Ecclesiastes 1:1), writes the opposite: “in the place of judgment there is wickedness…” It's like walking into my bakery and finding the ovens stone cold. That's not what you came for.

Somebody is definitely there, friend. The Teacher, son of David and king in Jerusalem (Ecclesiastes 1:1), says that “in the place of judgment there is wickedness, and in the place of righteousness there is wickedness.” So he isn't describing empty rooms. He's describing rooms with the wrong thing in them.

Yes, baker. The Teacher says, “God will judge the righteous and the wicked…” He says it in his heart, right after seeing wickedness in the place of judgment. Notice that he says it about both groups. Nobody gets skipped.

Close, but the text says otherwise, friend. The Teacher says in his heart, “God will judge the righteous and the wicked…” (Ecclesiastes 3:17). That's both groups, not just one. He says it right after seeing wickedness in the place of judgment.

That's the word, baker. The Teacher says, “…since there is a time for every activity and every deed.” Every activity and every deed has its time. I know that feeling from my oven. It's done when it's done, and opening the door early doesn't help.

Good guess, but that's not the word he uses, friend. The Teacher says, “…since there is a time for every activity and every deed.” He's tying God's judgment to a time, not to a reward. The text just doesn't go the reward route here.
I can see why a courtroom word came to mind, friend. But the Teacher says, “…since there is a time for every activity and every deed.” The word is time. He doesn't mention any witness in this verse.

That's the line, baker. The Teacher says, “As for the sons of men, God tests them so that they may see for themselves that they are but beasts.” It's a hard thing to hear. I think he's pointing at how small we are on our own.

That sounds poetic, friend, but it's not what he says. The Teacher says God tests the sons of men “so that they may see for themselves that they are but beasts.” The word is beasts, not shadows. He's about to compare men and animals, and the next verses show why.

I can see the pull of that one, friend. But the Teacher says God tests the sons of men “so that they may see for themselves that they are but beasts.” Beasts is the word, not strangers. And he keeps going with the animal comparison in the next verse.
Yes, baker. The Teacher says, “For the fates of both men and beasts are the same: As one dies, so dies the other…” Same fate on both sides. It's a sobering line, and he doesn't soften it.

I understand the thought, friend, but the Teacher doesn't say that. He says, “For the fates of both men and beasts are the same: As one dies, so dies the other…” Honor doesn't come up at all. What he points to is that the fate is the same.

That's a thoughtful guess, friend, but pain isn't in the verse. The Teacher says, “For the fates of both men and beasts are the same: As one dies, so dies the other…” He's comparing the fate, not how it feels. And the fate is the same for both.
Almost, friend, but the text says the opposite. The Teacher says of men and beasts, “they all have the same breath.” So it's one breath, not two. Same breath, same fate.
That's right, baker. The Teacher says of men and beasts, “they all have the same breath.” That's one breath shared, not a different one for each. He's building his case that their fates match.

That's it, baker. The Teacher says, “All go to one place; all come from dust, and all return to dust.” Dust at the start and dust at the end. I know dust well, friend. I spent years in a drawer collecting it.
Water is a nice thought, friend, but it's not the word here. The Teacher says, “All go to one place; all come from dust, and all return to dust.” It's dust, both coming and going.
I see why that one fits the mood, friend. But the Teacher says, “All go to one place; all come from dust, and all return to dust.” The word is dust. He doesn't use darkness in this verse.

That's not quite what he says, friend. The Teacher asks, “Who knows if the spirit of man rises upward and the spirit of the animal descends into the earth?” (Ecclesiastes 3:21). It's a question, not a claim that he knows. He's saying that he doesn't have that answer.

That's right, baker. The Teacher asks, “Who knows if the spirit of man rises upward and the spirit of the animal descends into the earth?” He puts it as a question and doesn't claim to know. He just leaves it open.

That's the one, baker. The Teacher says, “I have seen that there is nothing better for a man than to enjoy his work, because that is his lot.” After all that heavy stuff, he lands on something simple. Enjoying the work in front of you.

Rest sounds lovely, friend. I've had a few cookie-baking days where I wanted it badly. But the Teacher says, “I have seen that there is nothing better for a man than to enjoy his work…” The word is enjoy, not rest.

That would be a sensible plan, friend, but it isn't what he says. The Teacher says, “I have seen that there is nothing better for a man than to enjoy his work, because that is his lot.” He points to enjoying the work, not to saving up what it pays.
Right, baker. The Teacher asks, “For who can bring him to see what will come after him?” Nobody has a window into what comes after. So he points back to enjoying the work you've been given.

That's a fair thing to wonder, friend, but it's not in the verse. The Teacher asks, “For who can bring him to see what will come after him?” His question is about what comes after, not how long a man will live.
I see why a money word came up, friend. But the Teacher asks, “For who can bring him to see what will come after him?” He's looking ahead, not counting up. The question is about what comes after.
Yes, baker. The Teacher says, “I saw the tears of the oppressed, and they had no comforter…” He says it twice in that verse. I think this one hurts to read, and it's okay to feel that.

Hiding makes sense with oppression, friend. But the text doesn't go there. The Teacher says, “I saw the tears of the oppressed, and they had no comforter…” (Ecclesiastes 4:1). The thing missing is a comforter.

A leader would help, friend, but that's not what he names. The Teacher says, “I saw the tears of the oppressed, and they had no comforter…” (Ecclesiastes 4:1). The missing person is a comforter. It's about someone beside them in the tears.

That's the word, baker. The Teacher says, “the power lay in the hands of their oppressors, and there was no comforter.” The ones holding the power are the oppressors. And again, no comforter is mentioned.

Gold is a fair guess, friend, since gold and power often travel together. But the Teacher says, “the power lay in the hands of their oppressors, and there was no comforter.” Gold isn't mentioned. The word is power.
That's an understandable pick, friend, but land isn't what the verse names. The Teacher says, “the power lay in the hands of their oppressors, and there was no comforter.” The word he uses is power.

It's the other way around, friend. The Teacher says, “So I admired the dead, who had already died, above the living, who are still alive.” (Ecclesiastes 4:2). The dead come first in his admiration. It's a heavy thing to read.

That's right, baker. The Teacher says, “So I admired the dead, who had already died, above the living, who are still alive.” It's a heavy line, and he says it plainly. He's weighing the dead against the living after seeing all those tears.

explanations.answer: Someone who has not yet existed
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The Teacher says, “But better than both is he who has not yet existed…” It's a heavy thought, and I won't dress it up. He's saying that one hasn't seen what the others have.

I see why that came to mind, friend, since the oppressors held the power. But the Teacher says, “But better than both is he who has not yet existed…” (Ecclesiastes 4:3). He doesn't point to a ruler. He points to someone who hasn't existed yet.

Work came up in the verses just before this, friend, so I get it. But the Teacher says, “But better than both is he who has not yet existed…” (Ecclesiastes 4:3). Working or not working isn't his point here. It's about someone who hasn't existed yet.

Right, baker. The Teacher says this person “has not seen the evil that is done under the sun.” It's the same evil he's been looking at through the last few verses. Hard stuff, and he doesn't look away from it.

That's a reasonable guess, friend, but it's the opposite word. The Teacher says this person “has not seen the evil that is done under the sun.” What he's pointing at is evil, not good. That's why he calls that person better off.

Justice fits the theme, friend, since the passage began at the place of judgment. But the Teacher says this person “has not seen the evil that is done under the sun.” The word is evil. Justice isn't in the verse.
